info.text: Quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: A connected graph has 12 vertices and 11 edges. How many components does it have?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. "Connected" means exactly one component: every vertex can reach every other.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
vector<vector<int>> adj = {{}, {2}, {1, 3}, {2}, {5}, {4}, {}};
vector<int> comp(7, 0);
int cnt = 0;
function<void(int)> dfs = [&](int v) {
    comp[v] = cnt;
    for (int u : adj[v]) {
        if (comp[u] == 0) {
            dfs(u);
        }
    }
};
for (int v = 1; v <= 6; v++) {
    if (comp[v] == 0) {
        cnt++;
        dfs(v);
    }
}
cout << cnt << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The groups are {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5} and {6} (an isolated vertex), so there are three components.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What is the largest number of components a graph with n vertices can have?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. With no edges at all, every vertex is its own component.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
vector<vector<int>> adj = {{}, {2}, {1, 3}, {2}, {5}, {4}, {}};
vector<bool> seen(7, false);
function<int(int)> dfs = [&](int v) {
    seen[v] = true;
    int size = 1;
    for (int u : adj[v]) {
        if (!seen[u]) {
            size += dfs(u);
        }
    }
    return size;
};
cout << dfs(3) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. From vertex 3 the DFS reaches 2 and then 1. The component {1, 2, 3} has 3 vertices.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: A graph must be connected and has n vertices. What is the minimum number of edges it can have?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Each edge can merge at most two components, so going from n components to 1 needs at least n - 1 edges.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
vector<string> g = {"#.#", "##.", "..#"};
int R = 3, C = 3;
vector<vector<bool>> seen(R, vector<bool>(C, false));
function<int(int, int)> fill = [&](int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || r >= R || c < 0 || c >= C) return 0;
    if (g[r][c] != '#' || seen[r][c]) return 0;
    seen[r][c] = true;
    return 1 + fill(r + 1, c) + fill(r - 1, c) + fill(r, c + 1) + fill(r, c - 1);
};
int islands = 0, largest = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) {
        int s = fill(r, c);
        if (s > 0) {
            islands++;
            largest = max(largest, s);
        }
    }
}
cout << islands << " " << largest << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The cells (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1) touch each other and form one island of 3. The cells (0,2) and (2,2) are alone, so there are 3 islands and the largest has 3 cells.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Connected component  →  [[1]]

Isolated vertex  →  [[2]]

Flood fill  →  [[3]]

Island  →  [[4]]

Union-Find  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words are the vocabulary of the lesson.

The correct answer:

  • Connected component → Vertices joined to each other and to nothing else
  • Isolated vertex → A component of size 1
  • Flood fill → Spreads from a cell to all connected cells
  • Island → A component of land cells
  • Union-Find → Merges components and tracks them quickly

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int parent[5] = {0, 1, 1, 3, 3};
int a = 4, b = 2;
while (parent[a] != a) {
    a = parent[a];
}
while (parent[b] != b) {
    b = parent[b];
}
cout << a << " " << b << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Vertex 4 points to 3, and 3 points to itself, so its representative is 3. Vertex 2 points to 1, which points to itself, so its representative is 1.

questiontext.text: Which traversal can be used to find the connected components?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Any traversal that visits everything reachable from a start vertex works, so DFS and BFS both give the same components.

questiontext.text:
Components are {1,2,3}, {4,5} and {6}. What does adding each edge do?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

3-4  →  [[1]]

5-6  →  [[1]]

1-6  →  [[1]]

1-2  →  [[2]]

4-5  →  [[2]]

2-3  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. An edge joining two different components merges them. An edge whose ends are already in the same component changes nothing.

The correct answer:

Merges two components: 3-4, 5-6, 1-6
Changes nothing: 1-2, 4-5, 2-3

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 2 (a graph that starts with 4 components).

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The count starts at n, one merge lowers it to 3, and the print shows 3 - 1 = 2. The lines depend on each other in this order.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int n = 4;
int comps = n;
comps--;
cout << comps - 1 << endl;

name.text: Q17 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operation into the gap so that merging two different components lowers the count (the output should be 4).

main.cpp
int components = 5;
int a = 1, b = 2;
if (a != b) {
    components[[1]];
}
cout << components << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Two different components become one, so the number of components decreases by one: 5 - 1 = 4.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int components = 5;
int a = 1, b = 2;
if (a != b) {
    components--;
}
cout << components << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with its job.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

comp[v] == 0  →  [[1]]

cnt++; dfs(v);  →  [[2]]

size[comp[v]]++  →  [[3]]

r < 0 || r >= R  →  [[4]]

components--  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These pieces appear in nearly every component program.

The correct answer:

  • comp[v] == 0 → The vertex has not been visited
  • cnt++; dfs(v); → Starts a new component
  • size[comp[v]]++ → Counts the size of a component
  • r < 0 || r >= R → Checks the grid boundary
  • components-- → One merge lowered the count

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int comp[7] = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
int components = 6;
int edges[3][2] = {{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {1, 3}};
for (auto& e : edges) {
    int a = comp[e[0]], b = comp[e[1]];
    if (a != b) {
        for (int v = 1; v <= 6; v++) {
            if (comp[v] == b) {
                comp[v] = a;
            }
        }
        components--;
    }
}
cout << components << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The first two edges each merge two different components (6 to 5 to 4). The third edge joins vertices that are already together, so nothing changes.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Does each graph have exactly one component?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

A path 1-2-3-4  →  [[1]]

A cycle of five vertices  →  [[1]]

A star with centre 1  →  [[1]]

Two separate triangles  →  [[2]]

Three vertices and a single edge  →  [[2]]

Ten vertices and no edges  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A path, a cycle and a star are all in one piece. Two triangles, a lone edge among three vertices, and edgeless vertices leave several separate parts.

The correct answer:

One component: A path 1-2-3-4, A cycle of five vertices, A star with centre 1
More than one component: Two separate triangles, Three vertices and a single edge, Ten vertices and no edges
